extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, philosophers of science, and critical thinkers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for recognizing and avoiding common errors in induction and generalization when forming scientific, historical, social, or philosophical conclusions. Emphasizes proper separation of observation and inference, limits of analogy, causation vs. correlation, and the dangers of over-generalizing from limited data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish perceptions from inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid intermixture of witnesses' inferences with their narrative of perceptions; separate the actual sensations/perceptions from the hypotheses or conjectures drawn from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced cross-examiners note witnesses often mix inferences with perceptions; Dugald Stewart: even illiterate observers' narratives ‘involve more or less of hypothesis.’ A 'simple and genuine specification' of phenomena unsophisticated by preconceived opinions is evidence of disciplined observation. Train to faithful interpretation of nature; where sensations are indifferent people habitually pass to inference without attending to the sensation itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from local order to remote/unobserved regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences from the order of nature known on Earth (or in the solar system) to remote parts of the universe are groundless unless warranted; phenomena elsewhere may follow different laws or none at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience cannot supply necessary conditions for establishing universal claims about remote domains. Be cautious inferring properties of unobserved regions from local observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid asserting universal negatives from absence of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: The non-existence of a phenomenon cannot be conclusively inferred merely because it has not yet been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of observed instances only shows no adequate cause has manifested itself so far; it does not prove such causes do not exist. Universal negatives (assertions of impossibility) are generally unjustified by mere experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assert impossibility only when grounded in mathematics or universal causality
rubrics_metrics.description: The only laws that warrant attributing impossibility are those of number and extension (mathematical necessities) and the universal law of causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may affirm with assurance that nothing will change if all antecedents remain the same; but adding new antecedents might alter outcomes. Use mathematical/structural necessity or demonstrated universal causal laws to justify impossibility claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reduce radically different phenomena to a single element
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories that attempt to resolve qualitatively different phenomena (different in kind, not degree) into one element or principle are necessarily false unless solid causal/accounting connections are shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be valid to show certain motions are conditions of heat/light/sensation, but proving motions as 'conditions' is not the same as explaining the qualitative nature (e.g., sensation is not explained away as motion). Respect inherent distinctions in consciousness and other qualitatively distinct phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid simple enumeration (inductio per enumerationem simplicem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization by mere listing of observed instances without proper elimination or exclusions is a weak, provisional induction and prone to contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon: simple enumeration is 'res puerilis' and concludes provisionally. Proper induction should separate nature by rejections and exclusions, and only after sufficient negative instances conclude affirmatively. Beware taking observed instances alone as conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical laws from causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat empirical generalizations (customary order of succession) as if they were laws of causation; empirical laws without causal grounding are limited and liable to exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical laws that show regular succession may be useful but are not ultimate; we should seek the causes producing the observed regularity to obtain true causal laws. Elevating empirical summaries to causal status leads to many bad inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring causation from mere conjunction (post hoc / cum hoc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conclude that A caused B merely because A preceded or co-occurred with B; temporal or casual conjunction alone is insufficient to establish causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inferring England's industrial pre-eminence was due to restrictions on commerce, or that national debt caused prosperity. Such single-instance conjunctions might be of some value if supported by other evidence, but alone they are weak. Require elimination of other antecedents and presumption from known properties of the agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false theory / oversimplified single-cause explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concluding from properties of one suspected agent that it is the cause of complex phenomena, while overlooking other co-existing agents, leads to false theoretical generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical examples: attributing all disease to blood viscosity or to chemical imbalance led to dangerous errors (e.g., Sylvius de la Boe at Leyden). In politics and other fields, attributing absolute goodness to particular institutions without reference to context is similar error. Be wary of single-factor causal theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using analogy — it gives only weak presumption unless causal linkage known
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments from analogy infer that what is true in a known case may be true in a similar case; but analogy at best gives a small and non-assignable increase in probability unless a causal connection is established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: inferring planets are inhabited because Earth is inhabited — resemblance (orbital shape, composition) does not show those properties are conditions for habitation. If a causal connection between the shared property A and the target property B can be shown, then the argument becomes a causal induction, not mere analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overrate the probative force of analogies even when they are correct
rubrics_metrics.description: Even correct analogical similarities are often overstated by reasoners who perceive few properties and thus overvalue them; beware overestimating how much an analogy supports a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This error is common among those with narrow imaginations who focus on a few analogies and ignore conflicting ones. Broader consideration of multiple analogies reduces tendency to overvalue any single one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring resemblance in one respect from resemblance in another where evidence disconnects them (false analogies)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fallacious to infer that because two cases resemble each other in property A they also share property B when there is no evidence (and possibly evidence to the contrary) connecting A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political example: analogizing paternal government to political despotism on the basis of irresponsibility ignores crucial differences like parental affection and superiority of experience. Such disanalogies make the analogy false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base conclusions on appeals to perfection or aesthetic notions
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that assume nature must be 'perfect' or conform to some preconceived standard of perfection (and thence infer laws) are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Pythagorean appeals to numerical 'perfection' (perfect numbers implying planetary counts), or assuming heavenly bodies must move in perfect circles because of an idea of perfection. Avoid teleological/aesthetic premises as grounds for scientific law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen analogical inferences by demonstrating partial causal/conditional connections
rubrics_metrics.description: An analogy is more probative if one can show A is one of a set of conditions from which B would result, or that A is an occasional effect of some cause known to produce B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such less-close degrees of connection can be shown, the existence of B becomes more probable. Where possible, convert analogical reasoning into causal reasoning by identifying causal mechanisms or conditional relationships.
